titlePlain: Capstone: Write a Real Architecture Decision
subtitle: Lesson 20 · The Full Toolkit, Applied Start to Finish

eyebrow: The scenario: a real, unresolved decision
code:
Northbeam's assistant answers every question, even on
weak retrieval matches -- sometimes confidently wrong.

Should the team add a CONFIDENCE THRESHOLD that routes
low-confidence answers to a human instead?

A. Static threshold  -- simple; may not generalize.
B. Learned classifier -- more accurate; needs labeled
                         data Northbeam may not have.
caption: Write your own ADR before reading further -- Context, Decision, Consequences, Alternatives.

code:
We will start with a static threshold (A), tuned
against a small manually-labeled sample -- and revisit
a learned classifier (B) once the static-threshold
period itself has generated enough labeled data.
caption: Option A isn't a dead end -- it's preparation for Option B.

code:
+ Ships quickly, no new model to build or maintain
+ The static period generates the data B would need
- One fixed cutoff won't generalize across question
  types -- accepted in exchange for shipping sooner

Rejected: Learned classifier from day one -- no labeled
  data yet.  No threshold at all -- the problem this
  ADR exists to solve.
caption: Every alternative gets a reason, not just the chosen option.

eyebrow: Honest disagreement is fine -- and this is a real interview
code:
Proposed B instead, because Northbeam actually has the
data? That's a legitimate, defensible call.

The point isn't matching the model answer's conclusion --
it's reasoning the way it reasons.

"Walk me through how you'd decide X" is one of the most
common Staff/Principal interview formats.
caption: Name the real trade-off. Be honest about what's unknown. Write it down.

subtitle: From writing code well to owning the decisions, incidents, standards, and roadmaps around it — the shift from senior engineer to architect-level technical leadership.
